legend: Small discohesive tissue fragments of epithelial cells lacking myoepithelial cells with scant possible bare bipolar nuclei in the background. From a low-grade ductal carcinoma in situ. (Giemsa)

A cellular smear with partially crushed tissue fragments of large cells with atypical nuclei and considerable cytoplasm. Dispersed similar cells and stripped similar pleomorphic nuclei are in the background. (Giemsa)
Small tissue fragments of cells with enlarged atypical nuclei, some vacuoles, and crush artefact, similar single dispersed cells, and irregular stripped nuclei. Low cellularity. (Giemsa)

Scattered highly atypical cells in a background of necrotic debris, suggesting at least a component of high nuclear grade ductal carcinoma in situ with or without invasive carcinoma. Some cytopathologists may categorize this as “Malignant”. Final excision showed high-grade ductal carcinoma in situ. (Giemsa)

High cellularity, crowded tissue fragments of cells with moderate N:C ratios, enlarged mildly pleomorphic nuclei, and no myoepithelial cells. Occasional similar dispersed cells and no bare bipolar nuclei in the background. Some cytopathologists would categorize this case as “Malignant”. From a case of papillary ductal carcinoma in situ. (Giemsa)
Atypical epithelial cells with nuclear enlargement and a moderate degree of pleomorphism, but low N:C ratios and dense granular cytoplasm, consistent with apocrine differentiation. (Pap)

A branching fibrovascular core lined by atypical apocrine cells, indicating a papillary lesion. A calcific fragment is present upper central, slightly out of the plane of section (Giemsa). Histology showed apocrine encapsulated papillary carcinoma.

A large tissue fragment with fine branching fibrovascular cores lined by sheets of epithelial cells with mild to moderate nuclear enlargement and pleomorphism and lacking myoepithelial cells. No bare bipolar nuclei in the background. From a case of encapsulated papillary carcinoma. (Giemsa)
Dispersed monotonous often columnar atypical cells with relatively bland nuclear features raising the possibility of a papillary ductal carcinoma in situ. (Pap)
Cohesive tissue fragments with low- to intermediate-grade nuclear atypia, some dispersal of single intact cells, and an increased N:C ratio. From a case of encapsulated papillary carcinoma. (Pap)

Highly cellular, showing monotonous atypical cells with low-grade nuclei dispersed and in minute tissue fragments, one of which shows nuclear palisading (mid right), raising the possibility of a papillary lesion. From an encapsulated papillary carcinoma. (Giemsa)

A large crowded cohesive tissue fragment of epithelial cells with increased N:C ratios. Small darker nuclei with some irregularity mimic a bimodal pattern. From a case of solid papillary carcinoma. (Giemsa)

diagnosis: Suspicious for malignancy. Solid Papillary carcinoma.
legend: This fragment also shows a monotonous cytology. There are no fibrovascular cores, but a few haemosiderin-laden macrophages are noted in the background. There are only scanty cells present for assessment but the features are suspicious for malignancy (Giemsa). (b)
Large atypical cells with a high N:C ratio and enlarged nuclei are present in partially crushed tissue fragments, precluding a definite diagnosis of malignancy. (Giemsa)
Necrotic debris with a rare single atypical, enlarged stripped nucleus, suggesting high-grade ductal carcinoma in situ, but definite diagnosis is not possible on this material. (Giemsa)

There are dispersed single atypical cells and small tubule-like structures composed of cells with bland rounded nuclei without apparent associated myoepithelial nuclei. Some possible background bare bipolar nuclei are seen, but these may represent epithelial nuclei stripped of cytoplasm. The features are suspicious of a carcinoma of low nuclear grade. In the setting of such low nuclear grade features it is prudent to regard the smear as suspicious rather than diagnostic of malignancy (Giemsa). Histology showed tubular carcinoma.

Small cohesive crowded tissue fragments with some smaller darker nuclei mimicking myoepithelial cells that do, however, have some irregularity are present with occasional dispersed cells but no bare bipolar nuclei, considered “Suspicious for malignancy”. From a tubular carcinoma. (Giemsa)
Histological section of the tubular carcinoma shows the low nuclear grade features which on cytopathology smears may mimic a benign process such as a radial scar (H&E).

Dissociated cells showing moderate nuclear pleomorphism and occasional prominent nucleoli, with poorly defined cytoplasm. Differential diagnosis includes granular cell tumour and apocrine carcinoma. Although typically apocrine cells show more distinct cytoplasmic borders, granular cells may on occasion mimic this appearance. (Giemsa)

This higher magnification image of the same case highlights the enlarged and variable nuclei. If the diagnosis of granular cell tumour is not considered the case may be misinterpreted as carcinoma, possibly of apocrine type (Giemsa).
Highly cellular with atypical cells readily identified, but there is prominent formalin vapour artefact and a definite diagnosis of malignancy cannot be made. (Giemsa)
